a102.speaker: Qamar Ahmad, President (Amir) of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama'at in Benin
a102.speech: Stated that during the audience the delegation he leads discussed with the head of the HAAC the association's current projects held back by Covid-19 and its future achievements: "Because of the situation linked to the coronavirus, we were unable to complete some of our projects in the health, water and humanitarian aid sectors...", saying he hopes to soon complete the works in question.

a102.speaker: Qamar Ahmad, Amir of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama'at in Benin
a102.speech: Announces other future actions, notably in the health sector, involving free cataract operations and many other social and humanitarian works, assuring that the population will be invited when the time comes.

a191.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a191.speech: Said that more than three million internally displaced people have returned to their areas of origin since January as a result of the reduction in violence in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, with more than two million displaced people from North Kivu and more than 600,000 from South Kivu having returned home.

a191.speaker: UN humanitarian aid coordination agency (report)
a191.speech: According to its report, the more than three million internally displaced people returned to their homes following the peace agreement between the DRC and Rwanda.

a260.speaker: Amnesty International
a260.speech: Accused the Israeli government of "criminalising" the provision of humanitarian aid and of "attacking the rights of Palestinian refugees", by banning the operations of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

a260.speaker: Agnes Callamard, Secretary-General of Amnesty International (communique)
a260.speech: Stated that the Israeli decision is an "outrageous attack" which "clearly aims to make it impossible for the agency to function in the occupied Palestinian territories, forcing its closure in East Jerusalem and putting an end to visas for its staff" ; "It is a sign of the criminalisation of humanitarian aid and will only aggravate an already catastrophic humanitarian crisis", recalling that UNRWA "has played an indispensable role in providing water, food, health care, education and shelter to almost two million Palestinians in Gaza who have been forced to move" ; stressed that Palestinians face an "artificial famine" and "grave danger of genocide owing to Israel's continuous offensive over the past year" ; "UNRWA has been a lifeline for Palestinian refugees in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, as well as in neighbouring countries, since its founding 75 years ago. The suffering of the Palestinian people would have been even greater had it not been for UNRWA's work over three quarters of a century" ; called the ban "inhumane": "The Palestinians have already suffered unimaginably since the terrible attacks perpetrated by Hamas and other Palestinian factions against southern Israel a year ago" ; "The international community must swiftly condemn this decision and try to influence the Israeli government to take action."

a565.speaker: Fyawupi Mwafongo, Deputy Director for Disaster Response at the Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA)
a565.speech: Stated that the first batch of 4,000 metric tons of maize is already on its way to various districts across Malawi ; “This is not just about maize; it is about giving hope. For many families, this maize will be the difference between having a meal and going hungry,” stressing that the government’s approach is both practical and compassionate.

a565.speaker: Fyawupi Mwafongo, Deputy Director for Disaster Response at the Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA)
a565.speech: “We are not only focused on providing food, but also ensuring that families have access to nutritious food. This is a holistic approach to addressing hunger, and it involves collaboration with other stakeholders to ensure that the right food reaches the right people.”

a565.speaker: Cosmas Peleka, Operations Director at the National Food Reserve Agency (NFRA)
a565.speech: Said the agency has procured 83,000 metric tons of maize to distribute throughout the country, of which over 16,000 metric tons have already been delivered to DoDMA and an additional 5,874 metric tons released to ADMARC to help stabilize maize prices ; “Food security is a top priority for the government, and we are using every available resource to ensure that no one goes hungry. This maize will help to stabilize prices and ensure that food is available and affordable for all Malawians.”

a565.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a565.speech: Has called for national unity and collective responsibility in addressing the food crisis, urging all Malawians to play an active role in supporting government efforts ; “We must all stand together in solidarity to ensure that no one in Malawi goes to bed hungry. This is a national effort, and together, we can ensure that every Malawian has access to food, especially during these challenging times.”

a817.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of the Federal Republic of Somalia
a817.speech: In a speech delivered at the UN Food Systems Summit in Addis Ababa, presented the importance of international cooperation in fighting hunger, climate change and developing sustainable food systems; showed that Somalia has been affected by recurrent droughts and climate change, which has led millions of people to face hunger, and stressed that developing the system of crop and livestock production is indispensable in order to overcome these living conditions: “The Agricultural Development Strategy clearly sets out the importance of improving governance, increasing production, building economic infrastructure, developing agribusiness, and strengthening institutional capacity. I believe that agriculture does not only feed people, but also creates jobs, strengthens peace, and at the same time prepares a bright future for Somalia.” ; noted the Federal Government’s reconstruction-based plan (the National Transformation Plan), which gives priority to developing domestic production, growing the rural economy, cooperation between government and business, and building marketing systems that strengthen the links between farmers and domestic and international markets: “Food security is peace-building, and agricultural transformation is nation-building. Every investment made in it is an investment in building lasting peace and equitable economic growth.” ; called on the international community to strengthen its support for Somalia by providing backing for production infrastructure, the green economy and the implementation of modern agricultural technology so as to create food systems from which the Somali people can fully benefit.

a875.speaker: Government Assets Search Recovery Task Team (GASERTT)
a875.speech: Appearing before the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) this week, reported that one of its biggest red flags involves the suspicious transfer of government site 12284-569, near Pioneer Mall, to the Islamic Lesotho Maseru Central Mosque (ILMCM); according to the task team, the ILMCM’s original site measured only 2000 square metres, yet the compensation granted was a staggering 30,000 sqm, and the sites that ILMCM claimed had been affected were reportedly bought by government in 1998, a year before the road project began ; reported in its September progress report that it had finally managed to eject Mr Gan Quan.

a875.speaker: ‘Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, PAC chairperson
a875.speech: Challenged the explanation, questioning how ILMCM could have acquired land in an area already earmarked for construction ; “In Lesotho, a plan for a road takes more than five years, so for MCC to transfer a government site just a year before construction, shows there is fraud here. I think the government compensated a non-existent site.”

a875.speaker: ‘Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, PAC chairperson
a875.speech: Accused the recovery team of leniency, warning them against fuelling rumours that they were being bribed ; “I am disappointed that for the past three years you are yet to write to the occupants to evacuate. I suspect something fishy here . . . do not make us believe the rumours that you are taking bribes,” giving the team until 13 October to produce all documents regarding the site’s transfer.

a875.speaker: Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Lesotho
a875.speech: Is also demanding reports on allegations that the Basotho National Party (BNP) Centre and the Matekane Group Company (MGC) headquarters in Maseru were unlawfully built on government land.

a875.speaker: Gong Gan Quan, Chinese national, director of Chuye Construction
a875.speech: Insists his company had a right to the site since it was subcontracted by Anhoi Construction, the Chinese firm engaged to build the new State House completed in 2019; Chuye Construction remained, claiming they were doing “maintenance work” at State House; demanded M2 million compensation for “developments” he claimed to have made on the site.

a875.speaker: Moepana Kopo, GASERTT deputy chairperson
a875.speech: Dismissed those claims, saying Gan Quan even demanded M2 million compensation for “developments” he claimed to have made on the site ; “At one point, he claimed to have been maintaining the State House and that was not true . . . later he admitted that they were unlawfully occupying the place but asked for time to vacate,” Mr Kopo told PAC ; insisted Mr Gan Quan was eventually ejected.

a875.speaker: Moepana Kopo, GASERTT deputy chairperson
a875.speech: Said that when the task team attempted to eject him, they were blocked by Prime Minister’s Office PS, ‘Mabataung Khalane, who claimed she was relaying instructions from Minister Limpho Tau; further testified that their efforts to arrest Mr Gan Quan sparked backlash from senior officials, alleging that Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Limpho Tau and Communications Minister Nthati Moorosi intervened and ordered Mr Gan Quan’s release from police custody ; “We were even called to a meeting with Minister Tau, Minister Moorosi and PS Khalane, clearly to reprimand us. We were told to leave the Chinese man alone and drop the charges, but we made it clear to them that obstructing us will haunt them personally.”

a875.speaker: ‘Mabataung Khalane, Principal Secretary in the Prime Minister’s Office
a875.speech: Later denied stopping the eviction, insisting she only intervened because the team had allegedly arrived at the property “heavily armed”.

a875.speaker: ‘Mapeo Matlanyane, Director of Administration in the Prime Minister’s Office
a875.speech: Contradicted him: “The Chinese is still occupying the place; his properties are still in the house. Last week, my maintenance team found the Chinese still using the house. Neighbours confirmed that he arrives late and leaves early,” Ms Matlanyane told PAC ; later said the current occupants included two officials from the Federation of National Olympic Committees (FNOC), earmarked as the next legal tenants, as well as a security guard left behind by Gan Quan.

a1159.speaker: Hon. Deng Dau, member of the South Sudanese national parliament
a1159.speech: Called for urgent intervention to de-escalate tension in Eastern Equatoria, particularly in Magwi County following recent cattle camp violence that left several dead; said the First Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly convened a meeting with the Greater Bor Caucus on Monday to discuss the situation and that the meeting emphasized the need for social cohesion and coexistence between communities ; "Our message is that we need social cohesion between our communities. What has happened has happened and we say it should not escalate to cover and to continue as a source of insecurity to those that are outside this particular place." ; "We are one nation and one people. If there's anything that has happened, it can be addressed using our structures of the government. We have a police, we have a national army, and we have the governors and the commissioners to be able to address this particular situation."

a1159.speaker: Hon. Deng Dau, member of the South Sudanese national parliament
a1159.speech: Condemned inflammatory statements on social media, warning that they fuel hostility and division ; "We call upon the social media, particularly those who are fabricating and who are talking about more attack, mobilizing, more killing, they should stop this because it doesn't help us as people of South Sudan." ; Further urged youth and diaspora communities to use social media responsibly, advocating for peace rather than escalating tensions.

a1159.speaker: Hon. Deng Dau, member of the South Sudanese national parliament
a1159.speech: Urged the national government to coordinate with state and local authorities to enhance security and provide humanitarian assistance to affected communities; also called for swift action from security agencies and appealed for constructive dialogue to resolve conflicts between pastoralists and farmers.

a1275.speaker: Members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) (statement)
a1275.speech: have expressed their concerns about Sudan's catastrophic humanitarian crisis and acute food insecurity. In a statement seen by The City Review on Sunday, the 15-member Council raised alarm over the persistent transgressions of international law in Sudan and the severe consequences of the conflict on civilians, women, and children. The Council members applauded the ongoing discussions between the Sudanese warring parties that were arranged in Geneva by the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy, Ramtane Lamamra. ; They called on the warring parties in Sudan to respect international humanitarian law and human rights legislation, by ensuring the safety of civilians, notably in El Fasher, and by reducing hostilities and tensions. ; The Council members also urged the parties to seize the chance of the negotiations to decide on actions that will quickly accomplish these objectives and move toward a long-term resolution of the Sudanese situation. ; They appealed to the parties to reach an agreement on additional measures to permit and facilitate safe and unhindered humanitarian access into Sudan, in a way that complies with pertinent international law provisions and UN humanitarian assistance guiding principles, such as humanity, impartiality, neutrality, and independence. ; However, the Council encouraged all members to support mediation efforts for a lasting settlement rather than engaging in outside meddling that exacerbates conflict and instability.

a1331.speaker: William Ruto, Kenyan President and current rotating chair of the East African Community (EAC)
a1331.speech: Announced on 26 January that the extraordinary summit would be held within 48 hours, in consultation with the region's heads of state.

a1331.speaker: Felix Tshisekedi, President of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Paul Kagame, President of Rwanda
a1331.speech: Confirmed their participation in the summit.

a1331.speaker: Kinshasa (Congolese government)
a1331.speech: Accuses Kigali of actively supporting the M23.

a1331.speaker: Rwanda (government)
a1331.speech: Categorically denies the allegation that it actively supports the M23.

a1331.speaker: M23 (March 23 Movement, mainly Tutsi armed group)
a1331.speech: Accuses the Congolese government of failing to respect earlier peace agreements, which it gave as its reason for taking up arms again at the end of 2021.

a1331.speaker: Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations
a1331.speech: Urged Rwanda to cease all support for the M23 and to withdraw its troops from Congolese territory.

a1331.speaker: UN Security Council
a1331.speech: Condemned the violation of the DRC's sovereignty and called for an immediate de-escalation.

a1353.speaker: Institute of International Education
a1353.speech: According to the Institute, the United States draws over 1.1 million international students each year who contribute roughly $44 billion to the economy and sustain more than 378,000 jobs.

a1353.speaker: National Science Foundation
a1353.speech: Noted that foreign-born students make up one in five STEM workers in the U.S., addressing a domestic shortage of graduates in these critical fields.

a1353.speaker: A federal judge (court ruling)
a1353.speech: Temporarily blocked the attempt to revoke Harvard's ability to enroll international students.

a1353.speaker: Universities and advocacy groups
a1353.speech: Argue that the measures infringe on free speech and academic freedom.

a1353.speaker: China (government)
a1353.speech: Has publicly urged the U.S. to protect its students' rights; China has called for the protection of its students' rights, signaling potential diplomatic tensions.

a1353.speaker: European Union
a1353.speech: Has criticised Trump's policies as undermining global cooperation and has hinted at potential countermeasures, signaling broader diplomatic friction.

a1353.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1353.speech: Has expressed support for retaining talent, such as proposing green cards for foreign graduates during his campaign.

a1389.speaker: Du Xiaohui, Director General of the African Affairs Department of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1389.speech: In his presentation he returned to the origin of the creation of the cooperation framework that is the Beijing summit, which he describes as a historic event for Chinese diplomacy in the sense that never had so many heads of State and government gathered in its history. According to him, the relationship falls within a logic of necessity, namely the long-standing friendship uniting the two peoples, a natural outcome of Sino-African relations centred on solidarity, friendship, sincerity and treatment as equals.

a1389.speaker: Du Xiaohui, Director General of the African Affairs Department of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1389.speech: Enumerated the achievements of the cooperation: "Since the creation of FOCAC 25 years ago, it has been an example of the success of Chinese diplomacy, with 2,000 billion RMB yuan in trade, multiplied more than 25-fold, and more than one million new jobs. Five (5) visits to Africa by President Xi Jinping. Greater economic and commercial exchanges and 17.59 billion yuan to support domestic trade. China has made available to Africa several health specialists who have provided care to 1.6 million people in several countries. In the field of agriculture, two hundred (200) agronomists have been deployed to Madagascar, Eritrea and Burundi for the development and growth of agriculture. To help with governance, a platform for exchanging governance experience has been set up."

a1389.speaker: Du Xiaohui, Director General of the African Affairs Department of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1389.speech: On China's openness to the rest of the world, particularly to Africans, explained that his country has a policy that testifies to its willingness to promote unilateral openness, and that for China the visa policy is not a consular tool but an important tool for broadening its openness. "I have had exchanges with my colleagues and I have learned that discussions on visa exemption for Africans are still ongoing. The visa policy aims to promote exchanges between China and the rest of the world, but it also has the mission of ensuring a country's security, of maintaining balance, security and international cooperation, and a minimum of prudence is called for; but in any case China will remain determined to promote unilateral openness."

a1389.speaker: Du Xiaohui, Director General of the African Affairs Department of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1389.speech: In view of the recent Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic of Iran, stressed that our world is no longer peaceful, with these new examples.

a1389.speaker: Du Xiaohui, Director General of the African Affairs Department of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1389.speech: On cooperation between Niger and China, particularly in oil production and the difficulties the two partners have encountered in recent months, assured that in cooperation there is no situation that cannot be settled through dialogue. He stressed that Niger and China maintain deep friendly relations through a dialogue marked by mutual respect, and recalled the recent meeting in Changsha of the two foreign ministers, who discussed the question at length. "We consider that consultation and dialogue constitute the right path to follow in our trade exchanges, and disputes must be settled between friends and brothers. We are in friendly negotiations to ease this situation in order to send a positive signal to the rest of the world." He finally commended the efforts made by the Government of Niger to protect the oil installations at the cost of enormous sacrifices, notably the pipelines which, in places, have been sabotaged by armed groups.

a1558.speaker: Republicans in the US Senate
a1558.speech: Have said they will spare the US-backed HIV/Aids programme Pepfar from cuts, amid a larger effort to reduce government spending; senators said they would end a plan to cut $400m (£300m) from the President's Emergency Plan for Aids Relief programme, leaving total proposed cuts at $9bn.

a1558.speaker: BBC
a1558.speech: Reported that Republicans in the US Senate have said they will spare the US-backed HIV/Aids programme Pepfar from cuts.

a1558.speaker: Multiple senators from both parties
a1558.speech: Had expressed concern with cuts to Pepfar, which was launched under President George W Bush and has been credited with saving tens of millions of lives around the world.

a1558.speaker: John Thune, Republican Senate majority leader
a1558.speech: Said there had been a “lot of interest” in keeping the Pepfar funding intact.

a1558.speaker: Susan Collins, Republican Senator from Maine
a1558.speech: Told reporters after a White House lunch on Tuesday that she was “very pleased” that the cuts would be removed. Prior to the amendment, Collins had been vocal against the bill. She has not said whether the changes are enough to secure her support.

a1558.speaker: Russell Vought, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director
a1558.speech: Told reporters that the White House was on board with the Senate amendment, meaning that in its current form President Donald Trump would be willing to sign it.

a1610.speaker: Béatrice Radji, Vice-President of the Private Health Sector Platform of Benin (Pssp)
a1610.speech: Said the gathering is intended to be an opportunity for exchanges to contribute effectively to the improvement of the health system; believes the trust enjoyed by the actors of the private health system needs to be strengthened; recalled that the Pssp is an umbrella organisation of several associations whose objective is to contribute to improving the state of health of the Beninese population through a better organisation of private health sector actors ; said the Pssp also assigns itself the mission of ensuring the quality of the service offered in the private health sector, of building a partnership with the public sector and of contributing to the country's health policy, and maintained that these Days are a boon for better understanding the private health sector.

a1610.speaker: Jenelle Norin, Representative of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a1610.speech: "It is impossible to speak of the performance of this system and of its results while ignoring the private sector, especially because of the proportions it occupies in Benin's health system" ; added that strengthening the private system is as necessary as strengthening the whole system, which justifies USAID's support for the platform in order to raise the performance level of the health sector; said these Days represent a national space wanted by the actors to communicate on the current dynamics and on the progress made by the private health sector, and constitute an opportunity for exchange and for sharing knowledge and know-how.

a1610.speaker: Dr Raoul Saïzonou, representative of the World Health Organization (WHO) and lead of the technical and financial partners of the health sector
a1610.speech: Believes that this event is an opportunity to give and to receive, but also an occasion to review the many advances in the collaboration between the private and public health sectors; said the private sector offers very diversified resources and can help meet the demands placed on the public sector, as an integral part serving urban and rural areas, hence WHO's advocacy for it to be taken into account both in the drafting and in the implementation of national policies and plans; continued that in Benin the private sector's contribution to the provision of health services to the population is estimated at 60%.

a1610.speaker: Benjamin Hounkpatin, Minister of Health of Benin
a1610.speech: Estimated the private sector's contribution at more than 50% of the population's demand for care; maintained that, as part of the implementation of health system reforms, the government has initiated strong measures to clean up the sector, notably the closure of clandestine clinics, the issuing of authorisations of existence, control measures and the fight against counterfeit medicines; pleaded: "This strong will requires the commitment of the private sector and the harmonisation of practices between public and private. The two sectors must continue to strengthen their interventions for a public-private partnership that contributes to a strong and resilient health system." He gave the management of the Covid-19 pandemic as the perfect illustration of this successful collaboration.

a1610.speaker: Lucien Dossou-Gbété, President of the Private Health Sector Platform of Benin (Pssp)
a1610.speech: Will himself take charge of better presenting his organisation, explaining its genesis, its mission, its objectives and strategic axes.

a1639.speaker: Ritshidze survey/report (group of organisations representing people with HIV)
a1639.speech: A survey among more than 9 000 people from groups with a higher risk of contracting HIV shows that less than half, and in some cases not even a quarter, are greeted with a friendly face at health centres. In some of these groups about one in five people have been refused care ; When researchers from Ritshidze asked transgender people, men who have sex with men, sex workers and injecting drug users about how they're treated at government health centres, less than half, and in some cases not even a quarter, of the over 9 000 respondents reported being greeted by a friendly face. Moreover, in some of these groups, about one in five people said they've been blocked from getting health services.

a1639.speaker: Ritshidze report (recommendations)
a1639.speech: Recommended that the health department send out a circular to all clinics to explain that people from key populations should never be refused healthcare ; recommended that the health department should work with people from populations with high HIV infection rates, for instance sex workers or drug users, to develop posters that can sensitise health workers to those populations ; also pointed out that many transgender people said they wanted access to hormone therapy, but that this seems to only be available at large institutions in cities, while at clinics in rural areas people struggled to get it.

a1639.speaker: National health department of South Africa
a1639.speech: Says they know about this discrimination, and that they're rolling out training to help health workers see patients without judgement.

a1639.speaker: James Oladipo, one of the Ritshidze report's authors
a1639.speech: People from these groups have a high chance of getting HIV - and knowing that they will be discriminated against, they stop going to clinics altogether, he told Mia Malan in May.

a1639.speaker: Viyonce Mabena, trans woman who works at The Aurum Institute
a1639.speech: "Public health should be where we can run to," she says. But instead they get turned away.

a1639.speaker: Luyanda Mzimela, trans woman and counsellor at one of The Aurum Institute's POP INN clinics
a1639.speech: Recounts her experience of going to a government clinic: "I felt like I was not human. You've heard of human zoos [in European countries] back then? I felt like people looked at me like I'm an animal."

a1639.speaker: Thato Chidarikire, acting head of HIV programmes at the national health department
a1639.speech: Says the department deals with doctors and nurses who discriminate against patients who have a higher chance of contracting HIV by teaching them about being sensitive and trying to understand the cause of the issue.

a1639.speaker: Thato Chidarikire, acting head of HIV programmes at the national health department
a1639.speech: On who provides the training: "It's both. Most of the training happens through partners, but we also do some." ; On the training content: "We have a training curriculum. It has a participant's manual and a facilitator's manual. The first few chapters have an introduction to basic HIV information [for example, symptoms and prevention tools]. Then it introduces how to deal with clients, especially key populations, [for example] the LGBTQ community, sex workers, men who have sex with men. [This is part of the training so that health workers will] know how to respond and how to manage a situation [they are unfamiliar with]. We also train lay counsellors because they often do HIV testing." ; "This training has video clips [where real people share their] experiences. [For example] there's a chapter on transgender people, with a trans person talking about their experience at a [health] facility. Because of a lack of information, people [struggle to] understand [key populations]. [The curriculum] starts from the basics, from [people's] reality. What we're trying to [achieve is] to say, 'Be sensitive, be competent.'"

a1639.speaker: Thato Chidarikire, acting head of HIV programmes at the national health department
a1639.speech: On the circular recommended by the Ritshidze report: "I can confirm that the circular was signed and sent out."

a1639.speaker: Thato Chidarikire, acting head of HIV programmes at the national health department
a1639.speech: On educational materials: "We're working with partners who specifically serve key populations to develop education and communication material in the form of posters and pamphlets for both healthcare workers and communities." ; On the audience: "Anyone who uses public health facilities. [The idea is that] you will [see] posters on the walls that talk about different services that are provided by the facility. In the waiting rooms, you'll find pamphlets that can be taken home. We also distribute the material to communities [during outreach activities]."

a1639.speaker: Thato Chidarikire, acting head of HIV programmes at the national health department
a1639.speech: On investigating discrimination cases: "My office hasn't gone out to investigate [as such]. Because our community monitoring organisation works with provincial health departments, implementation happens at the district level, and that's where the investigations are supposed to happen. [The national department] then follows up to look at what the problems [are], especially logistics, because that's where we have power. For example, if a report says there hasn't been training, [it's something we will try to resolve]." ; On what happens if a worker is found to discriminate: "There would be an investigation, to get to the root cause. When we started [the] sensitisation programme with Pepfar [the US President's Emergency Plan for Aids Relief], we went to facilities and spoke to health workers about the training. [When we hear of discrimination, we explain that as a health worker] you don't judge, because it's not your job. You [should] give the services [that are needed] without any judgement."

a1639.speaker: Thato Chidarikire, acting head of HIV programmes at the national health department
a1639.speech: On access to hormone therapy in rural areas: "This is a specialised therapy [that is] scheduled and [people on it] also need psychosocial support. That's why it's in specialised facilities like tertiary hospitals [where there are specialist doctors]. [With] our [new] HIV plan, which is [now] more community centred, we want to ensure that everyone gets the services they need. However, when we think about moving a service out of a clinic or hospital and into a community, we need to talk about the infrastructure, training, and how it's going to be done safely. It's a work in progress."

a1756.speaker: Joseph Okee, Lobone Payam Administrator
a1756.speech: Said more than 300 grass-thatched houses have been gutted in a week-long bushfire in Lobone Payam in Magwi County leaving hundreds of people without shelter; said the fire – which is believed to have first ignited in Uganda's Lamwo District – seared its way across to South Sudan and escalated to Magwi territory last week. Said the fire incident consumed homes, properties and unharvested farm produce, that no human casualty has been reported, but pets and livestock have died in the fire outbreak. "From 170 in two days and now 370 houses in one week. The number of households that got burned yesterday is not yet counted."

a1756.speaker: Joseph Okee, Lobone Payam Administrator
a1756.speech: Said hundreds of local residents have been left without food and shelter, and expressed frustration over lack of intervention to mitigate the raging fire, with his constant plea for help proving futile. "We have been reporting this issue to the county authorities and until now, no response, no intervention, and the people are suffering under trees. As I talk now, people are under the trees and left with no food." ; "The situation is worsening so much. The most affected are children and the mothers having nothing at all. So, it is now a huge problem I can't be able to solve, I got confused even where to raise my concern."

a1756.speaker: Joseph Okee, Lobone Payam Administrator
a1756.speech: Appeals to the relevant authorities for humanitarian assistance to the affected households. "I would like the government and authorities in Magwi to give a quick response to this community so that if they think I'm lying, let them send the assessment team to come and see and decide for interventions."

a1756.speaker: Magwi County authorities
a1756.speech: Were not immediately available for a comment.

a2032.speaker: Kamina Johnson Smith, Jamaica's Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade
a2032.speech: Has publicly expressed profound gratitude to the Government of Eswatini for its cooperation and the duty of care exercised in facilitating the safe and voluntary repatriation of deportee Orville Isaac Etoria to Jamaica. "We are pleased to welcome home Mr Etoria and we trust the Jamaican public understands and joins the government in respecting his desire for a quiet return." She emphasised that the well-being of Jamaicans overseas remains a constant priority for the Government of Jamaica and noted that this case serves as another clear example of the importance of international cooperation and the critical role played by Jamaica's diplomatic network in protecting the rights of its citizens abroad.

a2032.speaker: Kamina Johnson Smith, Jamaica's Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade
a2032.speech: Extended thanks not only to Eswatini but also to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) for its direct support, as well as to Jamaica's High Commission in Pretoria for their hands-on engagement. "Together, our combined efforts ensured Mr Etoria's safe return," she added.

a2382.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Djiboutian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation
a2382.speech: In his opening address, recalled the deep and strategic partnership binding the two countries since the establishment of American forces in Djibouti, which has translated over the years into the strengthening of bilateral relations in a variety of fields.

a2382.speaker: Geeta Pasi, Deputy Assistant Secretary for African Affairs, US State Department
a2382.speech: Delivered a speech welcoming the Djiboutian delegation on behalf of the Under Secretary of State for African Affairs, and underlined the usefulness of this political dialogue, which is a genuine platform for advancing the strategic partnership and for highlighting its many assets in stabilising the region and in creating economic opportunities for Djibouti.

a2382.speaker: The two government delegations (Djiboutian and American)
a2382.speech: Agreed to consolidate their cooperation in strengthening economic exchanges between the two countries and in favour of development.

a2382.speaker: US delegation (American side)
a2382.speech: Congratulated the Djiboutian side on the success recorded in improving the business climate in the latest “Doing Business” report, as well as in the area of the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing.

a2382.speaker: Djiboutian delegation
a2382.speech: Insisted on the many reforms undertaken over several years to create an attractive business climate in Djibouti, and proposed to the American side that they promote promising economic projects in the fields of hospitality, renewable energy and airport infrastructure thanks to the financing provided for by their various initiatives.

a2382.speaker: Hassan Omar Mohamed, Djiboutian Minister of Defence, in charge of Relations with Parliament
a2382.speech: Highlighted the commitment of the Djiboutian government and of his ministerial department to strengthening the partnership between the Djiboutian and American armed forces.

a2443.speaker: Note published in “Notícias Online” (Brazilian embassy announcement)
a2443.speech: Said the donation consists of one ton of dehydrated nutritional meals and five water purifiers, with the capacity to produce 5,000 liters of drinking water daily ; according to the document, the event will be attended by representatives of INGD, the Brazilian embassy and the Pedagogical University of Maputo (UP), which will facilitate the installation of the equipment in Cabo Delgado.

a2492.speaker: Jonuel Gonçalves, economist and academic
a2492.speech: Told Expresso das Ilhas: "It is always better to have positive rather than negative percentage growth, although it is worth stressing that these are percentages applied to rather low base values" ; "It will be important at the end of the exercise to publish the full amounts of the respective GDPs and the effects on the HDI [Human Development Index]."

a2492.speaker: Victor Fidalgo, economist and international consultant
a2492.speech: "In my 50 years of following African affairs, I have witnessed countless declarations from both African leaders and institutions and non-African institutions, each more euphoric than the last, feeding hopes, dreams or illusions about the immediate rebirth and strengthening of African economies" ; "And it was precisely in the last 20 years that we saw Africa, as a whole, sink further. The end of apartheid in South Africa, as well as the end of the civil war in Angola, did not bring the leveraging of regional economies that had been dreamed of. Large countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo fell into political and economic stagnation and immobility, or, like Sudan, were dismembered or are on the verge of being so."

a2492.speaker: UNECA and African Development Bank (AfDB) documents/reports
a2492.speech: According to the documents, Niger and Senegal are expected to record significant economic growth due to increased production and exports of hydrocarbons; growth in Niger will also be driven by the recovery of agricultural production and increased crude oil output; growth in Senegal will be driven by an increase in private and infrastructure projects; growth in the DRC will be driven by the extractive sector owing to the opening of new oil fields, as well as by agriculture, services and mining; Rwanda's growth will be driven by private consumption and investment, while Côte d'Ivoire's growth will be driven by increased investment resulting from pro-competitive market reforms and improvements in the business environment. The report shows that the continent is expected to grow from 2.8% in 2023 to 3.5% in 2024, reaching 4.1% in 2025, sustained mainly by net exports, private consumption and gross fixed investment.

a2492.speaker: Jonuel Gonçalves, economist and academic
a2492.speech: Explains that "in most cases, with the extractive sector remaining dominant and much of the infrastructure geared towards it, dependence on international prices for both exports and imports also persists, since domestic capacity to meet basic needs will remain limited. It would be important to increase this capacity with strong agro-industrial programmes, even making use of infrastructure that serves mining extraction and transferring profits from the latter to the former" ; "The imperative lies in technological innovation; changing this performance increases domestic productivity and makes it possible to take advantage of demand in the international market."

a2492.speaker: Victor Fidalgo, economist and international consultant
a2492.speech: Analyses that "Africa occupies a very subordinate place in the International Division of Labour, contributing low added value to the world economy. Suffice it to say that although it has 17.2% of the world's population, Africa contributes only 1% of world GDP and about 2% of global trade transactions. Therefore, African countries are at such a low economic level that they would need to maintain a growth rate close to double digits for 25-30 years in order to improve or balance their current position. To speak of the economic growth of Niger or Rwanda as good signs for Africa is worse than claiming that Luxembourg or Portugal could leverage the European economy... the five largest African economies (Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Algeria and Morocco) are still unable to leverage the rest, which is why it is somewhat utopian to expect Africa's position in the global balance of power to change in the next 15-20 years."

a2492.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) figures
a2492.speech: Project growth of Cabo Verde's national economy at 4.5%, slightly below the estimates of the government and the Central Bank, which point to 4.7% this year.

a2492.speaker: International Monetary Fund (World Economic Outlook, published 16 April)
a2492.speech: Estimates Cabo Verde's GDP growth at 4.7% in 2024, while inflation falls from 3.1% in 2023 to 2% in 2024.

a2492.speaker: Jonuel Gonçalves, economist and academic
a2492.speech: "Cabo Verde is on this line of prospects. Either it stays at percentage growth rates that do not really advance, or it moves to innovation generating substantial growth in full figures" ; "In Cabo Verde, initiatives in the areas of basic pharmaceuticals, assembly and finishing of solar panels, semiconductors, with the appropriate insertion of artificial intelligence, are within reach if the scale calculations are done and if financial conditions have more margin. This does not mean abandoning tourism. On the contrary, a much-visited democratic country is attractive to investors and international official negotiators. For those who look at the world from the South Atlantic, Cabo Verde can be more visible through up-to-date initiatives."

a2492.speaker: Victor Fidalgo, economist and international consultant
a2492.speech: Stresses: "I would like to correct this thesis that Cabo Verde depends on tourism. Until the end of the 1980s, our economy depended on nothing but foreign aid, emigrants' remittances and rain when it came. We had an economy entirely dependent on random factors and we were very poor, particularly in rural areas. It was from the 1990s that the new regime then installed, seeking leverage for our economy, dared to take the view that tourism could be the sector to drive our economy" ; "Today we would not have the international airports in São Vicente or Boa Vista without tourism... Therefore, the bet on tourism was one of the best decisions taken in the entire history of Cabo Verde, by Cabo Verdeans, since its existence" ; "We can say that thanks to tourism our economy is progressively bringing in new activities that are giving a new face and a new impetus to the Cabo Verdean economy. As for economic growth, we have still not managed to move beyond dreams. All the governments that have succeeded one another in Cabo Verde after 1991 promised double-digit growth rates and to reduce unemployment to single digits. Unfortunately, the policy measures adopted did not bring the promised results and it must be acknowledged that economic growth at the current pace (4-6%) satisfies neither the governments' promises nor Cabo Verdeans' ambitions."

a2492.speaker: Victor Fidalgo, economist and international consultant
a2492.speech: "The question of poverty and inequality, in most African countries, is still not on the agenda."

a2492.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, president of the African Development Bank
a2492.speech: Highlighted, when presenting the Outlook, that major changes in fiscal and monetary policy are still needed, as well as increased efforts to address internal and external imbalances, inflation and the debt problem.

a2492.speaker: Victor Fidalgo, economist and international consultant
a2492.speech: Reflects: "Before we talk about monetary and fiscal policies, we should look at the actual functioning of the state itself in African countries. In most African countries the state either does not work or, when it does, has many distortions and deficiencies that cannibalise the potential for economic growth. It is usually the small countries, without the capacity to influence, that give us an image of good functioning. But unfortunately, the sum of these small countries (Cabo Verde, Mauritius, Rwanda or Seychelles) does not define the overall African picture."

a2492.speaker: Jonuel Gonçalves, economist and academic
a2492.speech: Considers: "The assessment by the now moribund NEPAD (New Partnership for Africa's Development), made at the beginning of the millennium, pointing to 7% as the minimum continental average to reduce the lag, remains valid" ; "Nor is it news that it would be important to obtain moratoriums on external debt payments in order to free up, for two or three years, about 50% of the expenditure of a large part of public budgets, raising domestic credit capacity."

a2492.speaker: UNECA report and AfDB Outlook
a2492.speech: Are unanimous in their conclusions: boosting the growth of the African continent will require larger financing pools and various policy interventions.

a2568.speaker: Dr. Matthew Opoku Prempeh, Former Minister of Energy and Vice Presidential Candidate of the New Patriotic Party (NPP)
a2568.speech: Has stated that without the introduction of the Gold for Oil programme in 2022, Ghana’s economy would have been on the verge of collapse; said the initiative played a crucial role in conserving the Bank of Ghana’s foreign exchange reserves and reducing the burden of foreign currency shortages in the downstream petroleum sector ; explained that the forex required by Bulk Distribution Companies (BDCs) was straining the Bank of Ghana’s reserves, and that this pressure often forced BDCs to turn to the black market, driving up fuel prices.

a2568.speaker: NPP manifesto (presented at the CBOD Town Hall Meeting)
a2568.speech: Outlined plans to expand the Gold for Oil programme to ensure sustained fuel price stability, reduce forex pressure, and enhance liquidity in the downstream petroleum market; also detailed steps to strengthen the National Petroleum Authority (NPA) by enhancing its regulatory capacity and promoting an export-oriented petroleum hub.

a2568.speaker: Nana Amoasi, Chief Executive Officer of the Institute for Energy Security (IES)
a2568.speech: Disagreed with the former minister, arguing that the programme did not fully achieve its intended objectives.

a2568.speaker: Chief Executive Officer of the Chamber of Bulk Oil Distributors (CBOD)
a2568.speech: Noted that the town hall meeting served as a platform to engage the NPP on their policies for the downstream petroleum sector.

a2570.speaker: Calicious Tutalife, Senior Programs Officer responsible for Value Chains at the SADC secretariat
a2570.speech: Said the Southern African Development Community recognises the importance of collaboration among its member states as it assists in facilitating regional integration ; “Sadc recognises the importance of member states talking to one another. We can only be a region if we are able to collaborate and thus the only way we can achieve regional integration by working together” ; emphasized the necessity for member states to actively [engage] with one another, observe how peers are performing, learn how they tackle challenges, and collectively explore opportunities for sharing and collaboration ; “The main objective, particularly for the leather value chain, is that as member states we are at different developmental stages. By engaging and listening to one another, we can identify how to collaborate more effectively, not just by learning from each other” ; emphasized that while SADC may prioritise collaboration with one or two geographically proximate member states, partnerships with distant nations remain equally viable where synergies exist or shared priorities align ; “That’s precisely why we have established this forum thus to foster greater collaboration and enhance the competitiveness of the leather value chain across our region.”

a2570.speaker: Calicious Tutalife, Senior Programs Officer, SADC secretariat
a2570.speech: Said the export figures were still low, saying they view this as an opportunity to develop strategies to enhance regional performance: “The figures for exports are not impressive and we view this as an opportunity to develop strategies that enhance our regional performance,” without disclosing figures.

a2570.speaker: Calicious Tutalife, Senior Programs Officer, SADC secretariat
a2570.speech: Said the region was facing challenges in producing quality hides, as local farmers do not view animals as sources of hides, with most communal farmers raising livestock primarily for beef and dairy: “Traditionally, the core issue has been the quality of produced skins and hides. As you can appreciate, our animal husbandry and farming practices remain largely communal, compounding the challenge that farmers do not see animals as hide sources, thus undervaluing them,” adding that in some communities hides are treated as waste material and discarded ; “Consequently, accessing quality hides remains a major obstacle and we are keen to resolve this issue through engagements.”

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On the EU-Namibia partnership: "For me, the success of what we have managed together as the EU and Namibia is one of the very best examples of good cooperation between EU and our partners. This year, we celebrate 35 years of partnership between the EU and Namibia. I believe we built on trust, shared values, but also real results. Namibia is a strong democracy with stable institutions. That makes our cooperation natural... we are building a partnership on mutual benefits, which focuses on concrete projects based on our shared priorities. That is what our Global Gateway is about... To give you one figure: the EU has mobilised around N$25 billion in investments in Namibia. It is expected to attract more than N$400 billion in private investment. That is nearly twice Namibia's gross domestic product. It shows the scale of what we can achieve together."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On the priorities of his visit: "First, to reaffirm how much Europe values Namibia as a democratic partner, but also as a country with incredible potential. Second, to show that the EU is fully behind Namibia's own priorities: creating jobs for young people, ensuring access to clean and affordable energy, and leading the way in the development of Namibia's clean industry. Third, to demonstrate what we call the 360-degree approach. It means we do not just build infrastructure but also invest in skills, training and stronger institutions so that we create a lasting, long-term development." ; "Fourth, I want to showcase what we can build together... Together with President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, I will inaugurate the Cleanergy Solutions project in Walvis Bay, which marks the start of green ammonia production... We will also hold a signing ceremony for the Namibia Institute of Mining and Technology. There, we are working on an IGNITE GH2 programme. It will re-skill 700 unemployed graduates and train 40 instructors so that Namibia has the skilled workforce it needs for this new economy." ; "This combination of infrastructure, jobs and education is how we turn potential into real opportunities for people."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On critical raw materials and green hydrogen: "Namibia has some of the best natural conditions in the world for renewable energy and it is very rich in critical raw materials. But what matters most is that these resources are used to create value and new opportunities on the ground here in Namibia... A good example is the HyIron project in Arandis. It is Africa's first zero-emission green iron plant using hydrogen produced here in Namibia. At full scale, it will produce 1 million tonnes of iron every year, cut almost 1.8 million tonnes of CO2, and create thousands of jobs - around 6 000 in construction and 900 permanent jobs. Already, more than 60 Namibian small and medium enterprises have been involved in the project."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On alignment of Global Gateway with Namibia's development goals: "I see Global Gateway and Namibia's plans - Vision 2030 and the Sixth National Development Plan - as very much aligned. Both are about jobs, inclusion and resilience. One example is the transformation of Walvis Bay port. With support from the Port of Antwerp-Bruges, we are preparing a master plan to make it a major hub for green hydrogen exports and logistics. Partnerships with the Port of Rotterdam and Port of Sinesare will create new green corridors from Namibia to Europe."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On other areas of cooperation: "Our cooperation is much broader than hydrogen or raw materials. In education, we have helped establish vocational centres in Nakayale, Eenhana and Valombola... In agriculture, we are investing in infrastructure in the Northern Communal Areas to improve livestock productivity and help farmers adapt to climate change... We also support governance and social issues. We work with the Anti-Corruption Commission of Namibia, and we fund campaigns against gender-based violence, together with the United Nations." ; "On conservation, we support the Kavango-Zambezi trans frontier area... In times of crisis, such as the recent drought, the EU supported Namibia's emergency response." ; "Finally, regionally, we work through the Southern African Development Community and the African Union on peace, security and cross-border infrastructure. Namibia's ports make it a natural driver of regional integration. We want to help strengthen that role."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On democratic governance, climate resilience and sustainable development: "For me, Namibia is a perfect showcase that democracy, human rights, the rule of law and sustainability go hand in hand with economic growth and new opportunities. Together with Namibia, we do not just talk about climate action, but we act... By developing projects like the Cleanergy Solutions hydrogen facility in Walvis Bay or the HyIron plant in Arandis, together with Namibia, we demonstrate real leadership on clean industrialisation. At the same time, we protect some of the world's most unique biodiversity... This combination of democracy, sustainability and innovation makes Namibia an excellent partner for the EU."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On inclusive growth and local content: "We make sure our investments translate into real opportunities for Namibians. That is why our projects are linked to skills training, jobs and opportunities for local businesses. Through IGNITE GH2 at the Namibian Institute of Mining and Technology, we are re-skilling 700 unemployed graduates and training 40 instructors so that young Namibians can take up jobs in the hydrogen sector. The TIDRET solar programme brings clean electricity to vulnerable households - 70% of them women-headed - showing that the green transition must be inclusive."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On long-term priorities for the partnership: "Looking to the future, I want Namibia to become Africa's leader for clean industry with local value chains that generate quality jobs, boost businesses and drive growth. Europe is already Namibia's number one trading partner, with a positive trade balance for Namibia. But we want to go further. Our long-term priorities are clear: To work together on clean and sustainable industries that create local value and strengthen education and skills so young people can shape their future. All this is with strong focus on democratic institutions, anti-corruption efforts and the fight against gender-based violence. Ultimately, our vision is simple: for Namibia to thrive as a sovereign, prosperous partner that offers opportunities to its people and contributes to regional and global stability."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: Message to the people of Namibia: "Europe believes in the potential of EU-Namibia partnership. Your country has everything it takes - natural resources, democratic values and human talent to lead Africa's clean industrialisation. We have what is needed to support this ambitious goal. Together with Namibia, we will turn your potential into concrete opportunities. Together, we can build a partnership that will not only bring jobs and opportunities here but also inspire the rest of Africa."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On translating partnerships into tangible development outcomes: "For us, the real measure of our partnership is whether it brings new benefits to the people on their daily lives. That is why we always link our big investments with human development. Alongside flagship projects in green hydrogen and critical raw materials, we fund programmes in education, training, gender equality and support for civil society. This is our 360-degree approach... We also believe strongly that trade is a driver of development. By opening markets, strengthening value chains and supporting fair and sustainable business practices, trade creates jobs, boosts incomes and brings in investment. In the end, this also means more revenue for the government to provide public services in education, health and rural development. Our goal is clear: economic growth must go hand in hand with social progress."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On balancing development assistance with democratic governance, transparency and human rights: "For us, development and democracy always go together. All our partnerships, including with Namibia, are built on respect for human rights, democratic values and the rule of law. That means our support is not only about projects, but also about stronger institutions, more transparency and civic participation. A good example is our recent EUR2 million EU grant to strengthen transparency, community engagement and environmental governance in the hydrogen and extractive sectors. The programme brings together partners like DW Akademie, Namibia Development Trust and the Namibia Nature Foundation, making sure communities and civil society can hold decision-makers accountable and have a real say in how these new industries develop."

a2676.speaker: Jozef Sikela, European Union Commissioner for International Partnerships
a2676.speech: On Namibia's role in regional integration within SADC: "The EU is itself a regional union, so we know how important integration is. We strongly support SADC, the African Union and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). Through our Economic Partnership Agreement with six SADC countries, including Namibia, we already have a strong trade framework that gives access to EU markets and promotes regional value chains. Namibia, with its ports and strategic location, is especially well placed to drive this integration. Right now, we are supporting discussions between Namport and the Port of Antwerp-Bruges on developing the North Port area of Walvis Bay into an industrial hub, including for hydrogen. We are also working with the Port of Rotterdam on the expansion of Luderitz. Under Global Gateway, we are backing strategic corridors, such as Walvis Bay-Maputo, which will strengthen connectivity, boost intra-African trade and allow the region to fully benefit from the AfCFTA."

a2726.speaker: Federal Government of Nigeria
a2726.speech: Has called for stronger South-South cooperation and deeper health partnerships within the BRICS bloc to tackle pressing global health challenges.

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako (Dr. Tunji Alausa), Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Stressed that “global health is currently faced with several interconnected challenges,” including the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), antimicrobial resistance (AMR), pandemic threats, shrinking health funding, climate change, and civil unrest ; called on BRICS nations to work in solidarity, saying, “These challenges call for stronger South-South cooperation and more global solidarity to share best practices and resources to achieve the UN Sustainable Development Goals and create a more equitable world.”

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Described Nigeria’s participation in the BRICS health platform as a strategic alignment with the country’s Renewed Hope Agenda, noting that the Tinubu administration had launched the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative (HSRII) ; “We are implementing the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative to operationalise the Renewed Hope Agenda of the President of the country.” “The initiative rests on four pillars: effective governance; efficient, equitable, and quality health systems; unlocking healthcare value chains; and ensuring health security.” ; said the government is driving reforms using cross-cutting strategies such as digitalisation, data management, strategic financing, smarter spending, and a new work culture.

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Said the country is investing in the revitalization of primary healthcare, pooled procurement systems, phytomedicine development, and wider coverage under social health insurance schemes ; “We are placing greater emphasis on domestic resource mobilization and increasing our capacity to produce pharmaceuticals and critical health inputs.”

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Highlighted Nigeria’s achievement in rolling out the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine: “As of May 2025, we vaccinated over 14 million girls. This represents the highest number of HPV vaccinations in a single round globally.”

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Disclosed that, in a move to reduce donor dependence, Nigeria budgeted an additional $200 million in 2025 to sustain its AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria Programmes in response to declining Official Development Assistance (ODA).

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: “We are addressing Sickle Cell Disease, Type 1 Diabetes, Rheumatic Heart Disease, and Childhood Cancers through the PEN-PLUS strategy. Nigeria currently leads implementation in the African region.”

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Announced that the country will host the next high-level Ministerial Conference on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) in June 2026 in Abuja.

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Called for increased collaboration within BRICS on pharmaceutical and biomedical research: “We welcome opportunities to collaborate with BRICS countries on pharmaceutical and biomedical research on NCDs, phytomedicine development, and academic exchanges.” “We are also open to partnerships to strengthen our domestic capacities to produce drugs, medical devices, and vaccines.”

a2726.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a2726.speech: Said the BRICS bloc has a critical responsibility to lead the global health agenda, stressing that cooperation among its members will drive progress toward achieving SDG 3: “Our collective efforts at addressing global health challenges would not only complement individual country efforts but serve as impetus to ensure SDG Goal 3 is achieved without leaving anyone behind.” “In the context of our shared humanity, we must work together. Humanity is one.”

a2751.speaker: Charles Robertson, Global Chief Economist at Renaissance Capital
a2751.speech: Questions how Russia can heavily invest in Africa's exploration and production of oil and gas for export: “It is evident that Russia or Kazakh oil competes with Libyan, Angolan or Nigerian oil. Russia or Kazakh gas competes with Algerian or Egyptian gas,” Charles writes.

a2751.speaker: Chakib Khelil, Algerian Energy Minister
a2751.speech: Observes: “only partners that can bring something to the project, not just money, should be there. Not every partner is welcome on board on the project.”

a2751.speaker: Sebastian Wagner, Executive Chair of the Germany Africa Business Forum
a2751.speech: Notes that Afreximbank's effort to create an African Energy Bank is a huge testimony of how Africa can enhance cooperation and leverage domestic solutions to optimize its oil and gas market: “What we want to see is African financiers rallying towards supporting the rollout of TSGP. Increased oil and gas exploration, production and assets development is what will bring Africa out of energy poverty by 2030,” Wagner says.

a2751.speaker: Reports (unnamed)
a2751.speech: According to reports, a Steering Committee made up of the three Ministers and Director Generals of the NOCs, established during the two-day meeting, will be responsible for updating the feasibility study for TSGP and will meet at the end of July 2022 in Algiers to discuss the progress.

a2751.speaker: Some experts (unnamed)
a2751.speech: Perceive Russia's Gazprom's negotiation with Nigeria about possible participation in the project as a bid to either sabotage or control the flow of gas from Africa into Europe.

a2755.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2755.speech: Initially explained that the agreement included signing a contract allowing the United States to mine rare minerals in Ukraine's land.

a2755.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2755.speech: Went straight to the point and demanded that President Zelensky enter into an agreement with Russia to end the war, failing which the United States would withdraw from the talks and would no longer fund or provide aid to Ukraine. ; Appearing angry, told Zelensky that he was not sufficiently grateful for the military and political support from the United States and that he was 'gambling' with World War Three. ; Insisted that a deal had to be made in order to obtain peace against his adversary Russia. ; Said Zelensky had no right to tell Americans how they should feel about peace and the ongoing conflict there; instead he should listen and obey what he is told.

a2755.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, President of Ukraine
a2755.speech: Answered Trump openly that he should not have "any agreement" with Russia's President Vladimir Putin. ; Asked, "What kind of diplomacy?"

a2755.speaker: JD Vance, US Vice President
a2755.speech: Intervened and began publicly rebuking Zelensky, telling him that the war should be ended through diplomatic means, and called Zelensky 'disrespectful'; together with Trump blamed Zelensky for being ungrateful for the aid the United States has given Ukraine over more than three years of war with Russia.

a2755.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (post on Truth Social)
a2755.speech: "Zelensky disrespected the United States in its cherished Oval Office." ; "We had a very important meeting today at the White House. Much was learned that could never have been understood without conversation under such fire and pressure." ; "It is amazing to see what comes out through emotion, and I have determined that President Zelensky is not ready for peace if America is involved, because he believes our support gives him great strength in negotiations. I don't want advantage, I want peace." ; Added that Zelensky "can come back when he is ready for peace."

a2755.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a2755.speech: Among the things he wants fulfilled before halting the fighting is that Ukraine accept that the seized areas - Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia, Kherson, Pokrovsk and Crimea (held since 2014) - are the legitimate property of Russia; that Ukraine drop its bid to join NATO, which he claims endangers Russia's security and borders; and that Zelensky call an election to legitimise his hold on power, claiming he governs under Martial Law, saying he would agree to come to the negotiating table if Ukrainians elect him by legitimate votes.

a2755.speaker: Parliament of Ukraine
a2755.speech: Strongly opposed the demand for elections; representatives and members of parliament voted and endorsed Zelensky as the legitimate President of the nation.

a2766.speaker: Reports (unspecified media reports)
a2766.speech: Suggest that the Trump administration plans to merge USAID with the U.S. Department of State, significantly reducing its funding and workforce.

a2766.speaker: Donald Trump, US President, and Elon Musk, his adviser
a2766.speech: Have criticised USAID, arguing that overseas spending does not represent value for American taxpayers.

a2766.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2766.speech: Has described senior USAID officials as "radical lunatics" and has long advocated for cutting foreign aid, a stance that aligns with his "America First" policy prioritising domestic interests over international commitments.

a2782.speaker: Fahad Aldosari, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso
a2782.speech: Reaffirmed his country's solidarity with the Burkinabè people in the ordeal of the security crisis.

a2782.speaker: Fahad Aldosari, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso
a2782.speech: Retracing the history of the reunification of the kingdom in 1902, hailed the visionary spirit of the late His Majesty King Abdulaziz bin Abdulrahman Al-Faisal Alsaud, who set the country on the path to prosperity; according to him this "wise approach" was continued by his successors ; stressed that today the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques His Majesty King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has in a few years succeeded in advancing the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and setting up major development projects in all fields, embodied in the Vision 2030 launched by His Royal Highness Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence.

a2782.speaker: Fahad Aldosari, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso
a2782.speech: Said the Saudi authorities understood very early on the importance of relations with the outside world, which is why the department of foreign affairs was the very first Saudi ministry through which the late King Abdulaziz strove to establish excellent diplomatic relations with brotherly and friendly countries around the world, and that it is in this dynamic that bilateral cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Burkina Faso was concretised in 1965: "This beginning was driven by exchanges of official visits between our senior officials, which made it possible to considerably accelerate the wheel of cooperation existing between our country, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and Burkina Faso, with a direct and tangible impact on the peoples of the two brotherly countries."

a2782.speaker: Fahad Aldosari, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso
a2782.speech: Indicated that within the framework of this cooperation the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has supported Burkina Faso to the tune of more than 225 million US dollars in humanitarian and development aid through more than 44 projects in various fields such as health, education, energy, infrastructure, transport, agriculture and food security, and that during the crucial phase of the Covid-19 pandemic the kingdom provided medical assistance worth one million US dollars ; "My country also offered the sum of 200 million euros for the benefit of the G5 Sahel. Added to this are other direct or indirect forms of aid offered by the leaders of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso."

a2782.speaker: Fahad Aldosari, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso
a2782.speech: Paid tribute to the defence and security forces and to the Burkinabè people for all the efforts made in the fight against terrorist groups to preserve the integrity of the territory: "We are always with the Burkinabè people and express to them our support in the fight against terrorism and Saudi Arabia. Our relations are very dynamic and embrace many areas of cooperation."

a2782.speaker: Fahad Aldosari, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Burkina Faso
a2782.speech: Thanked the Burkinabè government for having expressed its support for Saudi Arabia, which will host the Universal Exhibition - Expo 2030 to be held in Riyadh.

a2799.speaker: US President Donald Trump (Executive Order)
a2799.speech: Has decided to freeze all Aid to foreign countries except Israel and Egypt, and has introduced tariffs; exceptions that are free are funds meant for life saving medicines, ARVS and other. His Executive Order comes in the footsteps of another order withdrawing the USA from the World Health Organisation.

a2799.speaker: Leonce Ndakumana, Burundian Professor of Economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst
a2799.speech: Has studied the Politics of Aid and found that in fact instead of being a net recipient of Aid, as it is said, Africa is a net creditor to America and the world through its corrupt leaders.

a2799.speaker: ActionAid studies (“Real Aid”)
a2799.speech: Studies by Action Aid called Real Aid reached similar conclusions.

a2799.speaker: The wise men of Tongaland (proverb)
a2799.speech: Say, a fool says or does things before swallowing his own saliva.

a2941.speaker: Edgar Chibaka, UK-Malawi Chamber of Commerce (UK-MCC) Chairperson and Co-founder
a2941.speech: Described the launch as a "defining moment for Malawi-Scotland relations". "This is about building a new era of economic collaboration through diaspora-led initiatives," said Chibaka. "We're honoured to welcome Hon. Mumba and other distinguished guests to Edinburgh to celebrate this shared vision."

a2941.speaker: UK-Malawi Chamber of Commerce (UK-MCC)
a2941.speech: According to the UK-MCC, Minister Mumba's participation underscores the government's commitment to positioning Malawi as an attractive investment destination.

a2941.speaker: Dr. Thomas Bisika, Malawi's High Commissioner to the UK and Patron of UK-MCC
a2941.speech: "Malawi is open for business. As we work toward becoming a self-reliant, upper middle-income country, trade and investment will be central to that journey."

a2941.speaker: Stuart Brown, CEO of the Scotland Malawi Partnership
a2941.speech: Hailed the launch as a natural extension of the longstanding people-to-people ties between the two nations. "This initiative brings economic opportunity into the heart of our historic partnership. It's about ethical, inclusive trade that benefits both Malawi and Scotland for generations to come."

a2996.speaker: International Cospas-Sarsat Organisation (announcement at its virtual meeting)
a2996.speech: Announced at its virtual meeting held on 13 June the creation of an international working group specialising in the application of artificial intelligence in satellite search and rescue systems, to be chaired by the UAE.

a2996.speaker: National Guard Command of the UAE, represented by the National Search and Rescue Centre (working paper)
a2996.speech: Submitted a working paper to the sessions of the International Committee, on the basis of which the decision was taken, putting forward an innovative technical proposal aimed at integrating artificial intelligence technologies into the operations of the Mission Control Centre (MCC), increasing the efficiency of space-based rescue systems and improving the speed and accuracy of the response to distress signals.

a2996.speaker: International Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Search and Rescue Systems
a2996.speech: Highly praised the role of the UAE, its quality contribution and its proactive initiatives in using modern technologies to achieve international humanitarian rescue goals ; adopted a recommendation to create a joint working group chaired by the UAE to coordinate technical cooperation between member states and the relevant bodies.

a3048.speaker: Arega Shumete (PhD), economist and Ethiopian Economics Association member
a3048.speech: sees this move not as an embrace of economic liberalisation but a worrying slide towards austerity. He asserted that advanced economies could afford lean capital expenditure budgets since their critical infrastructure is mostly in place - an advantage Ethiopia cannot claim.

a3048.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a3048.speech: insisted that Ethiopia's economy is growing at an impressive clip, boasting of the highest growth rate in East Africa this year - around 6.5pc.

a3048.speaker: Leaders of the opposition party, the National Movement of Amhara (NAMA)
a3048.speech: questioned his administrative competence, calling his party's governance a "failed leadership". They cited the soaring inflation, instability, and burgeoning poverty as evidence of his administration's shortcomings.

a3065.speaker: Civil Empowerment and Rule of Law Support Initiative (CERLSI)
a3065.speech: Welcomes the announcement by the U.S. Government to carry out investigations on how funds allocated to Nigeria and other countries through the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) have been utilized in the past decade.

a3065.speaker: U.S. Government (announcement)
a3065.speech: Announced that it will carry out investigations on how funds allocated to Nigeria and other countries through the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) have been utilized in the past decade.
